segments.title: A Lottery of Souls: Introduction to Deronda's World

utterances.text: Welcome to Daniel Deronda Unpacked, a close reading of George Eliot's final and most ambitious novel.
Over the course of this series, we'll be living inside a book that is strange, capacious, and — I would argue — still underestimated.
It's a novel about identity and inheritance, about who gets to belong and who is cast out — and it's almost ferociously modern in its concerns.
To help us do it justice, I have three extraordinary guides with me today.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose specialty is the architecture of fiction — how the great novelists build their effects, sentence by sentence.
Eleanor, it's wonderful to have you.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real-world scaffolding — what the institutions actually were, what the law permitted, what it cost to be on the wrong side of it.
James, very glad you're here.

And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it again and again — she brings the experience of the lifelong reader, someone who has felt the novel's full emotional weight across many readings.
Caroline, welcome.
We're beginning today with Daniel himself — specifically with a scene from his boyhood that George Eliot places at the very centre of his formation.
Eleanor, I'd love to start with you — because Eliot opens this scene with a sentence that I think is one of the most arresting in the novel.
It really is extraordinary, and the more you look at it, the more deliberate it becomes.
Eliot uses the word 'burned' — not 'fixed' or 'lodged' — which tells you immediately this is a wound, not just a memory.
And then she builds the sensory picture with extraordinary care.

"One moment had been burned into his life as its chief epoch — a moment full of July sunshine and large pink roses shedding their last petals on a grassy court enclosed on three sides by a gothic cloister."
The roses are already past their peak — they're shedding their last petals.
There is a sense of something ending before Daniel even knows what the moment means.
And the gothic cloister enclosing the court — enclosing the boy — feels like architecture doing the work of fate.
Eliot does not waste a single image.
What strikes me is how precisely Eliot renders the social mechanics of the situation alongside that imagery.
Daniel is reading Sismondi's History of the Italian Republics — a real and serious historical work.
He is being educated as a gentleman's son — because that is how Sir Hugo has chosen to present him to the world.
But the very book in Daniel's hands contains the history of men born out of wedlock — the illegitimate sons of popes and cardinals who shaped Italian politics.
It is as though Eliot has placed the clue directly inside Daniel's education, and made him the last person to see it.
In Victorian England, illegitimacy was not merely a social embarrassment — it was a legal disability of considerable weight.
It affected inheritance rights, social standing, the very name a person was entitled to carry.
Daniel is beginning to understand, at thirteen, that he might be legally nobody.
And what undoes me, every time I read this, is Eliot's tenderness toward the boy even as she places him in such pain.
She gives us the exact texture of how a clever, bookish child processes catastrophe.
She writes that he could have talked with wisdom about men born out of wedlock — he had Shakespeare, he had history.
But he had never brought such knowledge into any association with his own lot.
That is exactly how children work — they can hold abstract knowledge and lived experience in entirely separate compartments until the moment the wall breaks.
And then Eliot has this line that I find almost unbearable in its precision.
"Some children, even younger than Daniel, have known the first arrival of care, like an ominous irremovable guest in their tender lives."
An irremovable guest.
Once care arrives in that form, in childhood, it never quite leaves the room.
And notice how Eliot immediately follows that universal observation with Daniel's specific version of it.
The new guest for Daniel carries, as she writes, an enigmatic veiled face.
It is not the specific grief of poverty — it is something he cannot yet name.
Then comes what I think is the structural masterstroke of this entire passage.
After all this anguish, Daniel simply picks up his book and walks away.
And what that act seeds is a disposition that will define him for years.
"The idea that others probably knew things concerning which they did not choose to mention, set up in him a premature reserve which helped to intensify his inward experience."
Premature reserve — that is the wound that doesn't show.
It drives his whole character, his watching, his sympathy — everything flows from this one July afternoon.
There's a passage later in the same chapter that I keep returning to, because it sharpens all of this with a very specific social dread.
Daniel goes to his chamber and begins systematically reconstructing the evidence — servants' remarks, casual observations, the family tree in the cabinet.
And he arrives at a particular fear that is distinctly Victorian in its texture.
"If his father had done any wrong, he wished it might never be spoken of to him: it was already a cutting thought that such knowledge might be in other minds."
It is not the fact of illegitimacy itself he most fears — it is the dispersal of the knowledge.
Does the valet know? Does the housekeeper? Does the bailiff who rode with him round the farms?
That is the particular horror of being a secret in a household where everyone serves: you cannot know who already knows.
What strikes me is how Eliot makes Daniel feel the injustice of it so acutely — and yet he turns that feeling entirely inward.
She compares his pain to a maimed boy who feels a crushed limb — for others merely an average accident, but for him the centre of everything.
And then she gives us this detail about the family tree in the locked cabinet that he longs to examine — but will not.
He stops himself, because he would never bring himself near even a silent admission of the sore that had opened in him.
That self-restraint, at thirteen, is heartbreaking.
He protects himself by protecting the secret — even from himself.
And what's remarkable is that this wound — this premature reserve — shapes not only Daniel's psychology but the entire moral architecture of the novel.
He becomes a person of almost preternatural empathy precisely because he has learned what it is to carry a hidden dread.

That is one half of Eliot's great double portrait — and in our next segment, we turn to the other half: Gwendolen Harleth, a woman trapped inside a very different kind of mirror, facing a world that offers her beauty and freedom as substitutes for everything that matters.

segments.title: The Mirror and the Mask: Gwendolen's Entrapment

utterances.text: In our last segment, we saw how Daniel Deronda sets up a world governed by chance and by performance — where who you appear to be may matter more than who you are.
That tension lives nowhere more vividly than in Gwendolen Harleth — and that's where we're turning now.
What I find so remarkable about Gwendolen in these early chapters is how Eliot lets us inside her fantasy life with genuine comic relish.
There's a passage in chapter nine where Gwendolen is essentially writing her own romantic screenplay — in real time, out loud, with full stage directions.
She imagines Grandcourt brought to his knees, and the comedy keeps escalating until it tips into something almost theatrical.
"My arrow will pierce him before he has time for thought. He will declare himself my slave—I shall send him round the world to bring me back the wedding ring of a happy woman."
She's not just fantasising — she's directing the scene, assigning every role, controlling every outcome.
And then the whole fantasy collapses into farce: Grandcourt rides off to find Miss Arrowpoint already married to a needy musician and Mrs. Arrowpoint tearing her cap off.
It's burlesque, but it's also a portrait of a mind that cannot tolerate outcomes it hasn't scripted.
That phrase — 'before he has time for thought' — is so telling.
Gwendolen's power, in her own imagination, depends on speed — on striking before reflection can intervene.
Which makes it all the more devastating when she finally meets Grandcourt — because he is the one man she cannot rush.
Eliot's description of him at that first meeting is one of the most unsettling portraits in the novel.
"It was not possible for a human aspect to be freer from grimace or solicitous wrigglings: also it was perhaps not possible for a breathing man wide awake to look less animated."
'A breathing man wide awake to look less animated' — that double negative does something chilling.
He isn't stiff. He isn't performing composure. He's simply — absent.
And yet Gwendolen's first registered thought is simply: 'He is not ridiculous.'
Which is perhaps the lowest imaginable bar — but it's the bar she has set, and he clears it.
Historically speaking, a man in Grandcourt's position — old money, probable title, no immediate need to please anyone — would have had very little incentive to perform warmth.
The marriage market of the 1860s rewarded wealth and status on the male side; charm was optional.
What Eliot is showing us, I think, is that Gwendolen's social education has prepared her to read one kind of man — and Grandcourt is a different kind entirely.
And Eliot is absolutely clear-eyed about the mechanism underneath all of this.
There's a parenthetical in chapter ten — just one clause tucked inside a longer sentence — that is one of her most precise psychological observations.
"for Gwendolen had not considered that the desire to conquer is itself a sort of subjection"
Those parentheses are doing extraordinary work — they signal that this is a truth Gwendolen herself cannot see.
The narrator steps around her consciousness to deliver a verdict she'd refuse to hear.
The very desire to remain unaffected is already a form of being affected — it's structurally brilliant.
And it compounds as the novel goes on, doesn't it.
By chapter thirty-five, Gwendolen is married — and the person who imagined sending men round the world is barely holding herself together.
Eliot gives her this passage that reads almost like a diagnosis — tender and unflinching at once.

"Poor Gwendolen was conscious of an uneasy, transforming process—all the old nature shaken to its depths, its hopes spoiled, its pleasures perturbed, but still showing wholeness and strength in the will to reassert itself."
That word 'poor' — it's so quietly devastating.
It's not condescending. It's the narrator reaching through the page and taking her hand.
And then: 'still showing wholeness and strength in the will to reassert itself.' She is broken, but not broken through.
There's a contrast worth drawing here, because the novel doesn't let Gwendolen's egoism stand entirely alone.
Catherine Arrowpoint — who exists partly as a foil to Gwendolen — makes a choice in chapter twenty-two that Gwendolen could never have made.
She chooses Klesmer, the musician — the man the world considers beneath her.
And she explains her reasoning with this extraordinary inversion of social logic.
"He is of a caste to which I look up—a caste above mine."
In four words she dismantles the entire hierarchy that Gwendolen has been navigating — and she does it without drama.
Gwendolen is trapped inside the social structure. Catherine, briefly, steps outside it.
That contrast illuminates something important about how Eliot distributes her moral intelligence across the novel.
Catherine gets four words and she earns them completely.
Gwendolen gets hundreds of pages — and they're all necessary, because her journey toward that kind of clarity is the long, agonising one.
The title of the novel is Daniel Deronda — but in craft terms, Gwendolen is the harder and perhaps more daring achievement.
Trapped inside a social structure — James put it precisely.
And that structure — the drawing room, the archery ground, the dinner table — is itself a kind of character in this novel.
In our next segment, we'll be asking how those social spaces actually work as instruments of power and constraint — for Gwendolen, and for everyone else caught inside them.

segments.title: Drawing Room Tyranny: Social Order and Constraint

utterances.text: We've been exploring how Gwendolen is trapped by her own image — the performance of self that becomes its own prison.
But there's a deeper constraint at work beneath the social surface — something more primal, more terrifying.
James, I want to come to you first, because you've been sitting with these passages about fear — genuine, gothic, visceral fear.
What is George Eliot doing when she reaches beneath the drawing room and finds that abyss?
What strikes me first is the precision of the social camouflage.
Gwendolen is ashamed of her terror — not because it threatens anyone else, but because it threatens her own myth of herself.
Eliot tells us that her ideal was, and I'll quote directly here,
"to be daring in speech and reckless in braving dangers, both moral and physical."
That word 'reckless' is doing enormous work — it's an aspiration, not a description.
What she actually experiences is the opposite — helplessness, cosmic insignificance, the terror of open space.
And this is not a private eccentricity — it is what the social order demands she suppress and deny.
That suppression is so painfully exact, isn't it.
The passage that stays with me — I've returned to it again and again — is that sentence about solitude.
"Solitude in any wide scene impressed her with an undefined feeling of immeasurable existence aloof from her, in the midst of which she was helplessly incapable of asserting herself."
'Immeasurable existence aloof from her' — that phrase is almost astronomical in scale.
Eliot literally tells us that the astronomy lessons at school used to make Gwendolen tremble.
But then someone walks into the room, and the vastness simply — vanishes.
Human eyes and ears restore her world.
Which is devastating when you realize that human eyes and ears are also exactly what imprison her.
Caroline has put her finger on something architecturally brilliant there.
Eliot has built a trap with two exits that are both locked from the outside.
Now look at what happens when the terror breaks through in company — in the charade scene.
The staging is exquisite: Klesmer strikes that thunderous chord, the panel flies open, the dead face appears in wax-light.
And then Eliot gives us this portrait of Gwendolen frozen:
"She looked like a statue into which a soul of Fear had entered: her pallid lips were parted; her eyes, usually narrowed under their long lashes, were dilated and fixed."
'A statue into which a soul of Fear had entered' — that is a gothic inversion of the Pygmalion myth.
She becomes, for one instant, entirely what she actually is — not the composed performer, but the terrified self beneath.
And Eleanor's point about the Pygmalion inversion opens onto something I find historically telling.
Gwendolen has been fashioned by her social world to be ornamental, composed, a decorative object in the drawing room.
The moment the panel opens, the statue cracks — and the company sees what lies beneath the performance.
Now this connects directly to Lydia Glasher — to the confrontation at Gadsmere.
Lydia speaks with, as Eliot puts it, 'a biting accent' and 'a determined abstinence from anything violent in tone or manner.'
That is the most chilling kind of social control — precision weaponised against its own victim.
And then Gwendolen sees, in Lydia's face, something she cannot name, only feel:
"it was as if some ghastly vision had come to her in a dream and said, 'I am a woman's life.'"
Five words.
'I am a woman's life.'
Lydia is not threatening her — she is simply showing her the future she is walking toward.
That line undoes me every time I read it.
Because what makes it so devastating is that Lydia is not wrong.
She has lived the version of the story Gwendolen is about to enter.
And Gwendolen proceeds anyway — which is part of the tragedy, and part of the indictment.
By the end, after Deronda leaves her for the last time, that accumulated terror finds its final form.
Eliot gives us this:
"She was a banished soul — beholding a possible life which she had sinned herself away from."
'Sinned herself away from' — not 'been barred from', not 'been denied'.
The agency is hers, and that is the cruelest thing Eliot can say about her.
Caroline is right — and there's a counterweight to all of this in Grandcourt himself.
Eliot gives us that extraordinary passage where Grandcourt sits in his drawing room and simply — does nothing.
Books on the table, untouched.
Eliot calls his state something like —
"a state of the inward world, something like premature age, where the need for action lapses into a mere image of what has been, is, and may or might be."
'Premature age' — he is calcified, and he's barely forty.
But the horror is that this inertia is also power.
His refusal to act, to want, to feel — it becomes the gravitational force that pulls everyone around him into orbit.
Gwendolen's terror is active, explosive, full of suppressed life.
His is a terror of pure vacancy — and somehow that's the more dangerous one.
Eleanor has identified what I'd call the asymmetry of egoism in this novel.
Gwendolen's egoism strains and panics and overreaches.
Grandcourt's egoism is described by Eliot as 'the main trunk of an exorbitant egoism' — static, immovable, self-sustaining.
He doesn't need to assert himself because the world has never, for a single moment, asked him not to.
That is not a psychological portrait only — that is a social system made flesh.
Social system made flesh — and yet the novel keeps finding, in among all this dread and constraint, moments of extraordinary comedy.
In our next section, we're going to look at how wit and evasion function as a kind of survival strategy — and ask whether the laughter in this novel is a refuge or just another form of the trap.

segments.title: Wit and Evasion: Comedy as Survival

utterances.text: We've been looking at how social order pressed down on the people in Daniel Deronda's world — the drawing room as a kind of cage.
But Eliot also gives us something else: a rich vein of wit, irony, and comedy — and it turns out those aren't just relief valves.
They're survival strategies, and sometimes something darker still.
Caroline, you've been sitting on what I suspect is a favourite passage — let's start there.
I have, and it's one I've loved for years without quite being able to explain why it's so funny.
It's from Chapter 22, where Eliot is defending Klesmer's attachment to Catherine Arrowpoint — who is not a conventional beauty.
Eliot begins by making a genuinely beautiful case for intellectual sympathy as the highest form of attraction.
But then she takes a rather sharp turn, and says of the more obvious, conventional beauty —
"The more obvious beauty, also adorable sometimes — one may say it without blasphemy — begins by being an apology for folly, and ends like other apologies in becoming tiresome by iteration."
That phrase — tiresome by iteration — is doing so much comic work while sounding utterly composed.
She's essentially saying: pretty faces get boring, and the footnote is Tannhäuser, Merlin, and Ulysses.
Each of them described, without ceremony, as a man of dull imagination who didn't know what else to do with himself.
What strikes me architecturally is that the comedy is entirely in the syntax.
Eliot doesn't announce a joke — she simply extends a subordinate clause past the point of decorum.
Look at the Ulysses aside: she says Calypso herself furthered his departure — already funny — and then keeps going.
Penelope is absorbed in worsted work, Telemachus is mean and pettifogging about the household accounts.
The joke is that Homer's great epic of fidelity is reframed as a story about a rather dull domestic arrangement — and Eliot delivers it in a single breath of perfect prose.
The wit earns its keep here because it's also making a serious argument about the social valuation of women.
Klesmer's attachment to Catherine Arrowpoint violated a very specific set of class and beauty expectations.
In mid-Victorian England, a woman's value on the marriage market was indexed quite literally to her physical appearance and family fortune — in roughly that order.
Eliot's comedy here isn't merely stylistic — it's a direct assault on that indexing.
She's using the apparatus of learned allusion — mythology, epic tradition — to demolish the convention, and doing it with a smirk.
That smirk is exactly the word.
And we see a completely different register of comedy in the scene with Hans Meyrick and Deronda in Chapter 37.
It's much more dramatic — a comedy of exposure, almost.
Deronda has been delivering what he imagines is a serious, cautionary speech about Hans's paintings getting public attention.
And Hans just — laughs.
Then he says, with that wonderful mixture of fondness and mischief —
"You never gave me an advantage over you before... My pictures are likely to remain as private as the utmost hypersensitiveness could desire."
He's not wounded — he's delighted to have caught Deronda being, for once, slightly ridiculous.
That line is such a precise comic mechanism.
Deronda's speech has inadvertently revealed that he cares intensely about Hans's reputation — more than Hans does.
The comedy inverts the power relation: the artist, the one who's supposed to be vulnerable, turns out to be perfectly at ease.
It's also a very affectionate portrait of a particular kind of self-knowledge.
Hans knows exactly how good his pictures are, and he's made his peace with it.
That's a kind of freedom Eliot consistently admires — more than she admires ambition.
Though comedy, in this novel, doesn't always stay light.
There's a moment in Chapter 51 — Deronda's mother, the Princess, explaining why she married — which begins almost as a kind of performance.
And then it curdles into something genuinely chilling.
Yes — that passage is extraordinary, and it has its own terrible comedy buried inside it.
The Princess has spent her life performing — on stage, in society — and now she describes her own marriage as a performance she gave herself.
She says —
"I made believe that I preferred being the wife of a Russian noble to being the greatest lyric actress of Europe; I made believe — I acted that part."
And then she says what drove it: 'It was because I felt my greatness sinking away from me, as I feel my life sinking now.'
The phrase 'made believe' is doing extraordinary work — it's the language of children's games, pressed into the service of a life-defining self-deception.
And there is something almost absurd about it — this great artist, playing house to avoid admitting her powers had faded.
Except Eliot won't let us laugh.
That repetition — 'I made believe... I made believe' — is one of the most nakedly theatrical moments in the novel.
The Princess is, at this moment, performing the confession of having performed.
We can't entirely trust her account — and Eliot doesn't ask us to.
The irony is structural: the most self-dramatising woman in the novel can only access truth by framing it as drama.
And then we get, in Chapter 66, a line that deploys wit as something close to weaponry.
Ezra Lapidoth confronts his father — who has returned after abandoning the family — and what he says is almost comically minimal.
Eliot tells us he speaks with — and I want to quote the setup as well as the words —
"a slow biting solemnity which made the word father a reproach"— and the words themselves are: "I know you — too well — father."
Four words — five if you count the father separately, which you must.
Each pause is a controlled detonation.
It's the purest example in the novel of what you might call negative wit — everything left out.
Ezra could deliver a speech.
He knows everything — the gambling, the betrayal, the years of abandonment.
Instead he gives nothing — except the word 'father,' loaded until it breaks.
Wit, evasion, self-performance, reproach compressed into a single word — these are all, in their way, strategies for navigating a world that won't give you a straightforward place in it.
Which brings us, naturally, to a question the novel keeps circling: what happens when the question of where you belong has its roots not in society's rules but in blood, faith, and history?
That's where we'll go next — into the novel's most searching territory: religion, identity, and the weight of inheritance.

segments.title: The Double Inheritance: Religion, Identity, and Belonging

utterances.text: We've just been exploring how comedy functions as a kind of armour in this novel — a way of surviving social pressure.
But there's another kind of pressure at work in Daniel Deronda — one that goes deeper than social manoeuvre.
This segment we're turning to questions of identity, inheritance, and where a person truly belongs — and the novel is extraordinarily searching on all three.
What strikes me first, coming into this part of the novel, is how Eliot sets up Deronda's situation with almost mathematical precision.
He is drawn toward Gwendolen — the narrator is quite frank about that.
But then comes this extraordinary sentence — and I want to read it exactly as Eliot wrote it.
"But his history had given him a stronger bias in another direction. He felt himself in no sense free."
Two sentences. That's all. And yet they contain the entire tragedy of Deronda's position.
He is not free — not because of external constraint, but because of something internal, something inherited, that he cannot yet even name.
And what makes that unfreedom so interesting historically is that Eliot won't let it be merely romantic.
The novel is asking a very serious question about what we inherit — not money, not property, but orientation, vocation, the shape of one's sympathies.
And crucially, Deronda's sympathies are shown to have very definite limits.
The narrator is merciless about this in the passage dealing with his feelings about Mirah's family.
Deronda prides himself — genuinely prides himself — on siding with the oppressed.
And yet when it comes to actual Jewish people, he has absorbed every ugly prejudice the culture has to offer.
Eliot doesn't excuse this. She names it.
And the naming is extraordinary. The line that stopped me cold on every re-reading is this one.
"But these fine words with which we fumigate and becloud unpleasant facts are not the language in which we think."
"Fumigate." She uses the word for treating an infestation.
The implication is that Deronda's high-minded language is a form of disinfection — covering over a smell he'd rather not acknowledge.
And then she turns the accusation outward — "we," not "he."
The reader is implicated. It's a very bold move.
That shift from "he" to "we" is one of the great rhetorical gestures in the novel.
Eliot does it elsewhere too — she pulls back the camera, widens the frame, and suddenly the specific psychological portrait becomes a general indictment.
And what follows that sentence is almost grotesque in its specificity — Deronda's imagination running through these lurid fantasies about Mirah's family.
A hawk-eyed woman, rough-headed and unwashed. A young Jew talkative and familiar.
Eliot is showing us the actual texture of prejudice — not the abstract principle, but the vivid, particular image that the prejudiced mind generates.
And she does so while also, carefully, providing a degree of mitigation — "Excuse him," the narrator says.
The phrase "it was the habit of his mind to connect dread with unknown parentage" ties Deronda's prejudice directly to his own wound.
He fears what Mirah's family might be partly because he fears what his own origins might reveal.
The prejudice and the identity crisis are not separate problems — they are the same problem, viewed from different angles.
Which is why, when the narrator then describes how Deronda feels about Gwendolen and Mirah simultaneously, it reads as genuinely moving rather than merely clever.
There's this passage — Eleanor, you flagged it — about the bird.
The narrator says Deronda would likely love a woman without ever telling her so, and offers this image.
"Sprinkle food before a delicate-eared bird: there is nothing he would more willingly take, yet he keeps aloof, because of his sensibility to checks which to you are imperceptible."
The image does something I find almost unbearably precise — it puts the failure to connect entirely within the character, not the circumstance.
It's not that Deronda can't love — it's that his sensibility is so finely tuned that the smallest check is felt as an impossibility.
And that quality — the reticent, principled, almost self-defeating capacity for feeling — is what makes the novel's other inheritance story so devastating by contrast.
Because Gwendolen has also inherited something — but hers is far more brutal.
The passage describing Grandcourt's hold over her after she reads Mrs. Glasher's letter — it's one of the most chilling things in the novel.
Eliot writes — and the precision here is remarkable —
"The definite dread was lest the veil of secrecy should fall between her and Grandcourt, and give him the right to taunt her."
"With the reading of that letter had begun her husband's empire of fear."
"Empire of fear" — two words, and the whole marriage is defined.
And what's terrifying is that Grandcourt barely needs to do anything — the fear governs her all by itself.
The word "empire" is doing enormous work, and I don't think it's accidental.
In the legal world Eliot is writing about, a husband's authority over his wife was not metaphorical — it was constitutional, contractual, almost absolute.
Gwendolen has signed herself over to a man she already knew to be morally compromised, and the secret knowledge of that fact is the very instrument of her imprisonment.
Compare Deronda's unfreedom — shaped by history, by vocation, by the pull of sympathies he cannot yet explain — and Gwendolen's unfreedom, shaped by a single catastrophic choice.
The novel is asking: which of these is harder to bear?
And I suspect Eliot thought both were necessary — that there is no freedom without inheritance, and no dignity without reckoning with what you've inherited.
And there's a dark comedy in how Grandcourt entered this story, which Eleanor might recognise.
Because his announcement of the whole marriage plan is delivered in five words.
He simply says: "I am going to marry the other girl."
"The other girl." Not her name. Not a description. Just — the other one.
The contempt in that phrase anticipates everything that follows in the marriage.
He's already reducing her to a category. And she's not even his wife yet.
That's the genius of Eliot's irony throughout — comedy that curdles as you look at it longer.
By the time we reach the empire of fear, we've forgotten we ever laughed at Grandcourt.
But Eliot hasn't forgotten. She built that laughter in as part of the trap — for Gwendolen, and a little for us.
Inheritance, then — of identity, of prejudice, of the consequences of a single choice — is everywhere in this novel.
Which brings us, naturally, to the question of what characters do with that inheritance — and what it costs them morally to look away.
In our next segment, we're going to follow that thread into the most uncomfortable territory of all — complicity, conscience, and the moral arithmetic of love.

segments.title: Complicity and Conscience: The Moral Arithmetic of Love

utterances.text: We've been exploring how identity — religious, national, inherited — shapes the characters of this novel in ways they barely understand.
But identity also shapes how people love — and how they fail to love — and that's where this segment takes us.
What strikes me first, and I keep coming back to this, is how early Eliot establishes Gwendolen as someone who experiences love as an intrusion.
There's that extraordinary moment with Rex — brief, almost throwaway — but it sets everything in motion.
She looks at him fiercely and says —
"Pray don't make love to me! I hate it!"
That word "fiercely" — Eliot doesn't give us wounded dignity or cold disdain, she gives us something almost feral.
And in two short sentences, Eliot has told us everything we need to know about Gwendolen's relationship to vulnerability.
That fierceness is doing a great deal of social work too, I think.
For a young woman of Gwendolen's position in 1865, love — or what passes for it — is inseparable from the transfer of legal and economic power.
To be "made love to" is literally the beginning of a process by which you hand over your autonomy.
Her hatred isn't irrational — it's a completely accurate reading of her situation.
And yet — and this is what makes her so compelling and so difficult — she walks straight toward exactly what she fears.
Eliot's narrator has this wonderful, gently devastating way of showing us Gwendolen's self-deception.
She refuses the burnous from Lush — a small, sharp gesture — and Eliot tells us —

"she, poor child, had no design in this action, and was simply following her antipathy and inclination, confiding in them as she did in the more reflective judgments into which they entered as sap into leafage."
"Sap into leafage." That image is almost tender — and slightly merciless.
Eliot is saying: her instincts are organic, they just grow — she doesn't choose them any more than a tree chooses its leaves.
That phrase "poor child" does so much in a single breath, doesn't it.
It's the narrator slipping in — not judgmental, but not innocent either.
There's genuine sympathy in it, and also a kind of cosmic irony — we know what's coming, even if she doesn't.
It's free indirect style at its most ethically loaded.
And then we get to the Grandcourt passages, which are where this novel becomes genuinely alarming.
Eliot gives us direct access to Gwendolen's deliberations — and they are, to put it plainly, a masterclass in motivated reasoning.
She has already decided; she is simply constructing a scaffolding of justification around the decision.
The central image Eliot uses is this —
"Gwendolen wished to mount the chariot and drive the plunging horses herself, with a spouse by her side who would fold his arms and give her his countenance without looking ridiculous."
The image is magnificent — and Eliot lets it sit there without commentary, which is the more devastating choice.
Because we can all see that a spouse who merely folds his arms is not a spouse at all — he is a prop.
And the horses are plunging — that's not a stable situation she's imagining for herself.
There's already danger built into her fantasy of control.
Eliot even shows us Gwendolen recognizing her own uncertainty — the phrase about "subjection to a possible self" is extraordinary.
She is terrified of what she might do.
And yet she proceeds — which is the most human thing in the book.
Gwendolen's moral arithmetic is all about control — and the terror of losing it.
But elsewhere in the novel, Eliot shows us what love looks like when control is entirely absent — when someone is stripped down to nothing but hope and faith.
Eleanor, you've been looking at Mirah's account of her journey — which is one of the most harrowing passages in the book.
It really is — and I think it doesn't get the attention it deserves, partly because readers sometimes find Mirah too purely sympathetic.
But this passage is not pure — it's genuinely gothic in its account of what her father and the Count were doing to her.
The sentence about the Count's smile — that it "went through me with horror" — is physically visceral in a way we don't always associate with Eliot.
But it's the ending that undoes me, structurally and emotionally.
Mirah has reached absolute zero — no mother, no money, no home, her trust in God failing — and then she says —
"That was how it was. When the evening came and the sun was gone, it seemed as if that was all I had to wait for."
"And a new strength came into me to will what I would do. You know what I did. I was going to die."
The syntactic simplicity of "I was going to die" — after all that journey, all that prose — is a complete shock.
The journey itself is worth dwelling on — the historical specificity is exact and brutal.
She walks a substantial portion of the way from Dover to London — a young woman alone, looking like, as Eliot puts it, a "miserable beggar-girl."
And she arrives to find that the street she was looking for has literally been demolished — the old city pulled down.
This is the 1860s — London was being ripped apart and rebuilt constantly.
For the dispossessed, for the immigrant, for the refugee, the city's modernization was erasure.
Mirah's mother isn't just absent — the very address where she might have been found no longer exists.
And then — the small grace that saves her before Deronda saves her.
The young workman on the train who never speaks — who simply, silently, slips a half-napoleon into her pocket.
Eliot gives him no name, no backstory — he simply appears and disappears.
I find that one of the most moving things in the entire novel — the anonymous kindness of a stranger.
It's conscience without motive — which is exactly what Gwendolen has not managed to develop.
That contrast is at the structural heart of the novel, I think.
And it plays out most quietly — most devastatingly — in that moment between Gwendolen and Deronda in chapter thirty-five.
He walks toward her expecting a smile, and instead she turns and gives him —
"such an appealing look of sadness, so utterly different from the chill effort of her recognition at table, that his speech was checked."
"His speech was checked" — Deronda, for once, has nothing to say.
And then there's this suspended moment — Eliot measures it against what observers could see, and what the characters themselves felt.
The phrase she uses for that moment — it's one I go back to again and again.
Eliot writes —
"for what was an appreciable space of time to both, though the observation of others could not have measured it, they looked at each other —"
"she seeming to take the deep rest of confession, he with an answering depth of sympathy that neutralized all other feelings."
"The deep rest of confession." That is what Gwendolen has been denied her entire life — someone simply receiving her.
Not managing her, not desiring her, not fearing her — just seeing her.
And yet — we should be honest — Deronda cannot give her what she needs for very long.
He has his own destiny to follow — his own identity that is, as we've been discussing, pulling him eastward.
The sympathy is real — I don't doubt that for a moment.
But it can't be the answer to her life — and I think Eliot knows that, and Gwendolen is beginning to know that too.
Which brings us to the question the novel keeps circling back to: once love — real or imagined — has done its damage, what's left?
What does it look like to act rightly, or to try to, when conscience arrives too late?
That's exactly where we're headed next — duty, redemption, and what Eliot dares to call the path forward.

segments.title: What Remains: Duty, Redemption, and the Path Forward

utterances.text: We've been tracing the moral cost of Gwendolen's choices — the slow, painful arithmetic of what love and complicity exact from a person.
Now I want to turn to what remains: the question of redemption, of duty, and whether the novel allows its characters — and its readers — any genuine path forward.
What strikes me most about the redemption arc in this novel is how stubbornly interior it is.
Eliot isn't interested in dramatic public gestures of atonement.
The transformation happens in exactly the unmapped, irrational, half-conscious terrain she keeps pointing us toward.
There's this extraordinary passage about Gwendolen and the necklace, where Eliot admits that even Gwendolen can't explain her own impulse.
And then she gives us this: — "There is a great deal of unmapped country within us which would have to be taken into account in an explanation of our gusts and storms."
That sentence is doing enormous work — it's not an excuse for Gwendolen, it's a claim about the limits of rational moral accounting altogether.
Eliot is saying: if you want to understand how people change, you have to go somewhere maps don't reach.
And what I find so moving is that Gwendolen keeps the necklace precisely because she cannot explain why.
That irrational clinging is the first genuinely unperformative thing she does in the novel.
Everything before has been about calculation — who is watching, what effect she is producing.
We see it so early — even that glorious quadrille scene, where she is carrying everything before her, is shadowed by the machinery of self-observation.
Eliot tells us she was 'one of the longest and widest sighted of mortals' — and yet she studiously pretended not to see who was watching her.
"she had been one of the shortest sighted instead of the longest and widest sighted of mortals."
That's Eliot's dry wit at its best — but it also indicts Gwendolen perfectly.
The necklace is the moment when she stops performing and simply feels.
I want to bring Deronda's mother into this, because she represents the absolute limit case of what Eliot is diagnosing.
The Princess is a woman who has made performance her entire ontology — she cannot stop acting herself, even in genuine suffering.
Eleanor called it 'unperformative' feeling — and that is exactly the capacity the Princess has forfeited.
Eliot describes it with clinical precision — and yet there is real compassion in the passage too.

"experience immediately passed into drama, and she acted her own emotions... each nucleus of pain or pleasure had a deep atmosphere of the excitement or spiritual intoxication which at once exalts and deadens."
'Exalts and deadens' — two words doing the work of a whole psychology.

The social history dimension here is real: this is a woman who was denied legitimate artistic ambition and was forced into a kind of permanent theatrical self-presentation as the only available form of agency.
What Eliot is showing, very quietly, is what it costs to live without interiority — without that unmapped country Eleanor was talking about.
And Gwendolen is in danger of becoming exactly that — until she isn't.
The Offendene passage near the end is one of the most structurally beautiful things in the novel, I think.
Eliot moves Gwendolen through this dissolving, dreamlike train journey — coal-pits, Gadsmere, a purgatorial blur — and then suddenly: Offendene.
The prose clears, the light changes, and we get this extraordinary sentence about what her marriage to Grandcourt actually was.

"a long Satanic masquerade, which she had entered on with an intoxicated belief in its disguises, and had seen the end of in shrieking fear lest she herself had become one of the evil spirits who were dropping their human mummery and hissing around her with serpent tongues."
'Human mummery' — I mean, that is devastating.
She sees that she could have become what Grandcourt was — a creature of pure performance with nothing beneath.
What saves her, I think — and I've argued about this with myself across many re-readings — is not Deronda's guidance exactly.
It's that Offendene, that memory of 'the breath of morning and the unreproaching voice of birds' — a self that pre-existed the masquerade.
The home she once fled from as dull becomes the image of what she might still recover.
Eliot is saying that innocence, even a dull innocence, leaves a trace — and that trace is what redemption follows back along.
The path forward, though — and I don't want to sentimentalise this — is genuinely uncertain.
Gwendolen is a widow with no money, no marriage prospects Eliot endorses, and a last letter from Deronda that essentially bids her farewell.
The novel leaves her exactly on the threshold — morally awakened, materially exposed.
Eliot understood that moral transformation and social rescue are not the same thing, and she refuses to conflate them.
That refusal to conflate them — I think that's what makes this novel so honest, and so lastingly uncomfortable.
Gwendolen earns her inner life and loses her outer world, and Eliot won't pretend those two things balance neatly.

We've covered so much ground today — from the comic machinery of Gwendolen's early self-deceptions, through the moral arithmetic of her marriage, to these final images of masquerade and morning light.
My warmest thanks to Eleanor Hartley, for showing us how the architecture of these sentences holds entire psychologies in place.
To James Blackstone, for keeping us honest about what the social world actually permits and what it forecloses.
And to Caroline Woodcourt, for reminding us that the best reason to read this novel is still the sheer pleasure of its sentences — the ones that make you stop, and go back, and read again.
And to you, for listening.
Daniel Deronda rewards every hour you give it — and then asks for more.

c16:p1.text:
Deronda’s circumstances, indeed, had been exceptional. One moment had
been burned into his life as its chief epoch—a moment full of July
sunshine and large pink roses shedding their last petals on a grassy court
enclosed on three sides by a gothic cloister. Imagine him in such a scene: a
boy of thirteen, stretched prone on the grass where it was in shadow, his curly
head propped on his arms over a book, while his tutor, also reading, sat on a
camp-stool under shelter. Deronda’s book was Sismondi’s  History
of the Italian Republics ; the lad had a passion for history, eager to know
how time had been filled up since the flood, and how things were carried on in
the dull periods. Suddenly he let down his left arm and looked at his tutor,
saying in purest boyish tones,
c16:p1.summary: Young Daniel, age thirteen, is reading history under his tutor Mr. Fraser's supervision when he innocently asks about the illegitimate children of popes and cardinals, beginning to suspect his own questionable birth.
c16:p1.best_quote: One moment had been burned into his life as its chief epoch—a moment full of July sunshine and large pink roses shedding their last petals on a grassy court enclosed on three sides by a gothic cloister.

c16:p10.text:
But at this moment on the grass among the rose-petals, Daniel Deronda was
making a first acquaintance with those griefs. A new idea had entered his mind,
and was beginning to change the aspect of his habitual feelings as happy
careless voyagers are changed with the sky suddenly threatened and the thought
of danger arises. He sat perfectly still with his back to the tutor, while his
face expressed rapid inward transition. The deep blush, which had come when he
first started up, gradually subsided; but his features kept that indescribable
look of subdued activity which often accompanies a new mental survey of
familiar facts. He had not lived with other boys, and his mind showed the same
blending of child’s ignorance with surprising knowledge which is oftener
seen in bright girls. Having read Shakespeare as well as a great deal of
history, he could have talked with the wisdom of a bookish child about men who
were born out of wedlock and were held unfortunate in consequence, being under
disadvantages which required them to be a sort of heroes if they were to work
themselves up to an equal standing with their legally born brothers. But he had
never brought such knowledge into any association with his own lot, which had
been too easy for him ever to think about it—until this moment when there
had darted into his mind with the magic of quick comparison, the possibility
that here was the secret of his own birth, and that the man whom he called
uncle was really his father. Some children, even younger than Daniel, have
known the first arrival of care, like an ominous irremovable guest in their
tender lives, on the discovery that their parents, whom they had imagined able
to buy everything, were poor and in hard money troubles. Daniel felt the
presence of a new guest who seemed to come with an enigmatic veiled face, and
to carry dimly-conjectured, dreaded revelations. The ardor which he had given
to the imaginary world in his books suddenly rushed toward his own history and
spent its pictorial energy there, explaining what he knew, representing the
unknown. The uncle whom he loved very dearly took the aspect of a father who
held secrets about him—who had done him a wrong—yes, a wrong: and
what had become of his mother, for whom he must have been taken
away?—Secrets about which he, Daniel, could never inquire; for to speak
or to be spoken to about these new thoughts seemed like falling flakes of fire
to his imagination. Those who have known an impassioned childhood will
understand this dread of utterance about any shame connected with their
parents. The impetuous advent of new images took possession of him with the
force of fact for the first time told, and left him no immediate power for the
reflection that he might be trembling at a fiction of his own. The terrible
sense of collision between a strong rush of feeling and the dread of its
betrayal, found relief at length in big slow tears, which fell without
restraint until the voice of Mr. Fraser was heard saying:
c16:p10.summary: Daniel sits motionless, his mind suddenly seized by the possibility that Sir Hugo is his father and that his birth is illegitimate, and he experiences acute emotional distress and shame, unable to speak or seek clarification.
c16:p10.best_quote: Some children, even younger than Daniel, have known the first arrival of care, like an ominous irremovable guest in their tender lives

c16:p12.text:
Daniel immediately moved the book without turning round, and after holding it
before him for an instant, rose with it and walked away into the open grounds,
where he could dry his tears unobserved. The first shock of suggestion past, he
could remember that he had no certainty how things really had been, and that he
had been making conjectures about his own history, as he had often made stories
about Pericles or Columbus, just to fill up the blanks before they became
famous. Only there came back certain facts which had an obstinate reality,
almost like the fragments of a bridge, telling you unmistakably how the arches
lay. And again there came a mood in which his conjectures seemed like a doubt
of religion, to be banished as an offense, and a mean prying after what he was
not meant to know; for there was hardly a delicacy of feeling this lad was not
capable of. But the summing-up of all his fluctuating experience at this epoch
was, that a secret impression had come to him which had given him something
like a new sense in relation to all the elements of his life. And the idea that
others probably knew things concerning which they did not choose to mention,
set up in him a premature reserve which helped to intensify his inward
experience. His ears open now to words which before that July day would have
passed by him unnoted; and round every trivial incident which imagination could
connect with his suspicions, a newly-roused set of feelings were ready to
cluster themselves.
c16:p12.summary: Daniel retreats alone, cycling through denial and acceptance of his suspicion, building a reserve that makes him listen intently to any remark that might confirm his fears and creating for himself a lasting emotional wound.
c16:p12.best_quote: And the idea that others probably knew things concerning which they did not choose to mention, set up in him a premature reserve which helped to intensify his inward experience.

c16:p19.text:
“Well, well, well!” said Sir Hugo, with surprised kindliness
intended to be soothing. But Daniel turned away quickly, left the room, and
going to his own chamber threw himself on the broad window-sill, which was a
favorite retreat of his when he had nothing particular to do. Here he could see
the rain gradually subsiding with gleams through the parting clouds which lit
up a great reach of the park, where the old oaks stood apart from each other,
and the bordering wood was pierced with a green glade which met the eastern
sky. This was a scene which had always been part of his home—part of the
dignified ease which had been a matter of course in his life. And his ardent
clinging nature had appropriated it all with affection. He knew a great deal of
what it was to be a gentleman by inheritance, and without thinking much about
himself—for he was a boy of active perceptions and easily forgot his own
existence in that of Robert Bruce—he had never supposed that he could be
shut out from such a lot, or have a very different part in the world from that
of the uncle who petted him. It is possible (though not greatly believed in at
present) to be fond of poverty and take it for a bride, to prefer scoured deal,
red quarries and whitewash for one’s private surroundings, to delight in
no splendor but what has open doors for the whole nation, and to glory in
having no privileges except such as nature insists on; and noblemen have been
known to run away from elaborate ease and the option of idleness, that they
might bind themselves for small pay to hard-handed labor. But Daniel’s
tastes were altogether in keeping with his nurture: his disposition was one in
which everyday scenes and habits beget not  ennui  or rebellion, but
delight, affection, aptitudes; and now the lad had been stung to the quick by
the idea that his uncle—perhaps his father—thought of a career for
him which was totally unlike his own, and which he knew very well was not
thought of among possible destinations for the sons of English gentlemen. He
had often stayed in London with Sir Hugo, who to indulge the boy’s ear
had carried him to the opera to hear the great tenors, so that the image of a
singer taking the house by storm was very vivid to him; but now, spite of his
musical gift, he set himself bitterly against the notion of being dressed up to
sing before all those fine people, who would not care about him except as a
wonderful toy. That Sir Hugo should have thought of him in that position for a
moment, seemed to Daniel an unmistakable proof that there was something about
his birth which threw him out from the class of gentlemen to which the baronet
belonged. Would it ever be mentioned to him? Would the time come when his uncle
would tell him everything? He shrank from the prospect: in his imagination he
preferred ignorance. If his father had been wicked—Daniel inwardly used
strong words, for he was feeling the injury done him as a maimed boy feels the
crushed limb which for others is merely reckoned in an average of
accidents—if his father had done any wrong, he wished it might never be
spoken of to him: it was already a cutting thought that such knowledge might be
in other minds. Was it in Mr. Fraser’s? probably not, else he would not
have spoken in that way about the pope’s nephews. Daniel fancied, as
older people do, that every one else’s consciousness was as active as his
own on a matter which was vital to him. Did Turvey the valet know?—and
old Mrs. French the housekeeper?—and Banks the bailiff, with whom he had
ridden about the farms on his pony?—And now there came back the
recollection of a day some years before when he was drinking Mrs. Banks’s
whey, and Banks said to his wife with a wink and a cunning laugh, “He
features the mother, eh?” At that time little Daniel had merely thought
that Banks made a silly face, as the common farming men often did, laughing at
what was not laughable; and he rather resented being winked at and talked of as
if he did not understand everything. But now that small incident became
information: it was to be reasoned on. How could he be like his mother and not
like his father? His mother must have been a Mallinger, if Sir Hugo were his
uncle. But no! His father might have been Sir Hugo’s brother and have
changed his name, as Mr. Henleigh Mallinger did when he married Miss
Grandcourt. But then, why had he never heard Sir Hugo speak of his brother
Deronda, as he spoke of his brother Grandcourt? Daniel had never before cared
about the family tree—only about that ancestor who had killed three
Saracens in one encounter. But now his mind turned to a cabinet of estate-maps
in the library, where he had once seen an illuminated parchment hanging out,
that Sir Hugo said was the family tree. The phrase was new and odd to
him—he was a little fellow then—hardly more than half his present
age—and he gave it no precise meaning. He knew more now and wished that
he could examine that parchment. He imagined that the cabinet was always
locked, and longed to try it. But here he checked himself. He might be seen:
and he would never bring himself near even a silent admission of the sore that
had opened in him.
c16:p19.summary: Daniel retreats to his chamber and spirals into conjectural reasoning about his birth, reconstructing casual remarks and observations as evidence of illegitimacy, questioning whether servants know his secret, and becoming obsessed with the family tree.
c16:p19.best_quote: if his father had done any wrong, he wished it might never be spoken of to him: it was already a cutting thought that such knowledge might be in other minds.

c9:p17.text:
“I know, but they demand thought. My arrow will pierce him before he has
time for thought. He will declare himself my slave—I shall send him round
the world to bring me back the wedding ring of a happy woman—in the
meantime all the men who are between him and the title will die of different
diseases—he will come back Lord Grandcourt—but without the
ring—and fall at my feet. I shall laugh at him—he will rise in
resentment—I shall laugh more—he will call for his steed and ride
to Quetcham, where he will find Miss Arrowpoint just married to a needy
musician, Mrs. Arrowpoint tearing her cap off, and Mr. Arrowpoint standing by.
Exit Lord Grandcourt, who returns to Diplow, and, like M. Jabot,  change de
linge .”
c9:p17.summary: Gwendolen elaborates an extended, witty fantasy in which she dismisses Catherine Arrowpoint's charms and imagines Grandcourt utterly conquered by her appeal, though ultimately frustrated and departing in humiliation.
c9:p17.best_quote: My arrow will pierce him before he has time for thought. He will declare himself my slave—I shall send him round the world to bring me back the wedding ring of a happy woman

c11:p1.text:
Mr. Grandcourt’s wish to be introduced had no suddenness for Gwendolen;
but when Lord Brackenshaw moved aside a little for the prefigured stranger to
come forward and she felt herself face to face with the real man, there was a
little shock which flushed her cheeks and vexatiously deepened with her
consciousness of it. The shock came from the reversal of her expectations:
Grandcourt could hardly have been more unlike all her imaginary portraits of
him. He was slightly taller than herself, and their eyes seemed to be on a
level; there was not the faintest smile on his face as he looked at her, not a
trace of self-consciousness or anxiety in his bearing: when he raised his hat
he showed an extensive baldness surrounded with a mere fringe of reddish-blonde
hair, but he also showed a perfect hand; the line of feature from brow to chin
undisguised by beard was decidedly handsome, with only moderate departures from
the perpendicular, and the slight whisker too was perpendicular. It was not
possible for a human aspect to be freer from grimace or solicitous wrigglings:
also it was perhaps not possible for a breathing man wide awake to look less
animated. The correct Englishman, drawing himself up from his bow into
rigidity, assenting severely, and seemed to be in a state of internal drill,
suggests a suppressed vivacity, and may be suspected of letting go with some
violence when he is released from parade; but Grandcourt’s bearing had no
rigidity, it inclined rather to the flaccid. His complexion had a faded
fairness resembling that of an actress when bare of the artificial white and
red; his long narrow gray eyes expressed nothing but indifference. Attempts at
description are stupid: who can all at once describe a human being? Even when
he is presented to us we only begin that knowledge of his appearance which must
be completed by innumerable impressions under differing circumstances. We
recognize the alphabet; we are not sure of the language. I am only mentioning
the point that Gwendolen saw by the light of a prepared contrast in the first
minutes of her meeting with Grandcourt: they were summed up in the words,
“He is not ridiculous.” But forthwith Lord Brackenshaw was gone,
and what is called conversation had begun, the first and constant element in it
being that Grandcourt looked at Gwendolen persistently with a slightly
exploring gaze, but without change of expression, while she only occasionally
looked at him with a flash of observation a little softened by coquetry. Also,
after her answers there was a longer or shorter pause before he spoke again.
c11:p1.summary: Gwendolen meets Grandcourt and finds him unlike her imagined portraits—physically handsome but emotionally inert, with an unsettling gaze and mysterious pauses that unsettle her usual self-mastery.
c11:p1.best_quote: It was not possible for a human aspect to be freer from grimace or solicitous wrigglings: also it was perhaps not possible for a breathing man wide awake to look less animated.

c10:p33.text:
Gwendolen chose to go too and be deposited in the same group with her mamma and
aunt until she had to shoot again. That Mr. Grandcourt might after all not
appear on the archery-ground, had begun to enter into Gwendolen’s thought
as a possible deduction from the completeness of her pleasure. Under all her
saucy satire, provoked chiefly by her divination that her friends thought of
him as a desirable match for her, she felt something very far from indifference
as to the impression she would make on him. True, he was not to have the
slightest power over her (for Gwendolen had not considered that the desire to
conquer is itself a sort of subjection); she had made up her mind that he was
to be one of those complimentary and assiduously admiring men of whom even her
narrow experience had shown her several with various-colored beards and various
styles of bearing; and the sense that her friends would want her to think him
delightful, gave her a resistant inclination to presuppose him ridiculous. But
that was no reason why she could spare his presence: and even a passing
prevision of trouble in case she despised and refused him, raised not the
shadow of a wish that he should save her that trouble by showing no disposition
to make her an offer. Mr. Grandcourt taking hardly any notice of her, and
becoming shortly engaged to Miss Arrowpoint, was not a picture which flattered
her imagination.
c10:p33.summary: The narrator analyzes Gwendolen's contradictory feelings toward Grandcourt, noting her claim of indifference masking genuine investment in his admiration, and her preference that he should pursue her despite her intention to reject him.
c10:p33.best_quote: (for Gwendolen had not considered that the desire to conquer is itself a sort of subjection)

c35:p126.text:
Poor Gwendolen was conscious of an uneasy, transforming process—all the
old nature shaken to its depths, its hopes spoiled, its pleasures perturbed,
but still showing wholeness and strength in the will to reassert itself. After
every new shock of humiliation she tried to adjust herself and seize her old
supports—proud concealment, trust in new excitements that would make life
go by without much thinking; trust in some deed of reparation to nullify her
self-blame and shield her from a vague, ever-visiting dread of some horrible
calamity; trust in the hardening effect of use and wont that would make her
indifferent to her miseries.
c35:p126.summary: Gwendolen is undergoing a transformative crisis: her hopes are spoiled, pleasures perturbed, but her will resists complete dissolution.
c35:p126.best_quote: Poor Gwendolen was conscious of an uneasy, transforming process—all the old nature shaken to its depths, its hopes spoiled, its pleasures perturbed, but still showing wholeness and strength in the will to reassert itself.

c22:p31.text:
“That is true,” said Catherine, with some betrayal of feeling.
“He is of a caste to which I look up—a caste above mine.”
c22:p31.summary: Catherine, with visible emotion, declares that the opposite is true: Klesmer's caste is one to which she looks up, placing herself beneath him rather than above.
c22:p31.best_quote: He is of a caste to which I look up—a caste above mine.

c6:p60.text:
The forgiveness was sooner bestowed than it would have been if Gwendolen had
not desired to dismiss from her own and every one else’s memory any case
in which she had shown her susceptibility to terror. She wondered at herself in
these occasional experiences, which seemed like a brief remembered madness, an
unexplained exception from her normal life; and in this instance she felt a
peculiar vexation that her helpless fear had shown itself, not, as usual, in
solitude, but in well-lit company. Her ideal was to be daring in speech and
reckless in braving dangers, both moral and physical; and though her practice
fell far behind her ideal, this shortcoming seemed to be due to the pettiness
of circumstances, the narrow theatre which life offers to a girl of twenty, who
cannot conceive herself as anything else than a lady, or as in any position
which would lack the tribute of respect. She had no permanent consciousness of
other fetters, or of more spiritual restraints, having always disliked whatever
was presented to her under the name of religion, in the same way that some
people dislike arithmetic and accounts: it had raised no other emotion in her,
no alarm, no longing; so that the question whether she believed it had not
occurred to her any more than it had occurred to her to inquire into the
conditions of colonial property and banking, on which, as she had had many
opportunities of knowing, the family fortune was dependent. All these facts
about herself she would have been ready to admit, and even, more or less
indirectly, to state. What she unwillingly recognized, and would have been glad
for others to be unaware of, was that liability of hers to fits of spiritual
dread, though this fountain of awe within her had not found its way into
connection with the religion taught her or with any human relations. She was
ashamed and frightened, as at what might happen again, in remembering her
tremor on suddenly feeling herself alone, when, for example, she was walking
without companionship and there came some rapid change in the light. Solitude
in any wide scene impressed her with an undefined feeling of immeasurable
existence aloof from her, in the midst of which she was helplessly incapable of
asserting herself. The little astronomy taught her at school used sometimes to
set her imagination at work in a way that made her tremble: but always when
some one joined her she recovered her indifference to the vastness in which she
seemed an exile; she found again her usual world in which her will was of some
avail, and the religious nomenclature belonging to this world was no more
identified for her with those uneasy impressions of awe than her uncle’s
surplices seen out of use at the rectory. With human ears and eyes about her,
she had always hitherto recovered her confidence, and felt the possibility of
winning empire.
c6:p60.summary: Gwendolen is relieved to forgive Isabel so she can dismiss the matter from her own mind. The narrator reveals that Gwendolen experiences occasional fits of spiritual dread unconnected to religious belief—a primal fear of cosmic solitude that she suppresses through human contact and the assertion of her will.
c6:p60.best_quote: Solitude in any wide scene impressed her with an undefined feeling of immeasurable existence aloof from her, in the midst of which she was helplessly incapable of asserting herself.

c6:p42.text:
Herr Klesmer, who had been good-natured enough to seat himself at the piano,
struck a thunderous chord—but in the same instant, and before Hermione
had put forth her foot, the movable panel, which was on a line with the piano,
flew open on the right opposite the stage and disclosed the picture of the dead
face and the fleeing figure, brought out in pale definiteness by the position
of the wax-lights. Everyone was startled, but all eyes in the act of turning
toward the open panel were recalled by a piercing cry from Gwendolen, who stood
without change of attitude, but with a change of expression that was terrifying
in its terror. She looked like a statue into which a soul of Fear had entered:
her pallid lips were parted; her eyes, usually narrowed under their long
lashes, were dilated and fixed. Her mother, less surprised than alarmed, rushed
toward her, and Rex, too, could not help going to her side. But the touch of
her mother’s arm had the effect of an electric charge; Gwendolen fell on
her knees and put her hands before her face. She was still trembling, but mute,
and it seemed that she had self-consciousness enough to aim at controlling her
signs of terror, for she presently allowed herself to be raised from her
kneeling posture and led away, while the company were relieving their minds by
explanation.
c6:p42.summary: As Klesmer strikes a thunderous chord, a hidden panel suddenly opens revealing a painted portrait of a dead face and fleeing figure in pale wax-light, causing Gwendolen to cry out in genuine terror and collapse.
c6:p42.best_quote: She looked like a statue into which a soul of Fear had entered: her pallid lips were parted; her eyes, usually narrowed under their long lashes, were dilated and fixed.

c57:p33.text:
He rose as he spoke, and she gave him her hand submissively. But when he had
left her she sank on her knees, in hysterical crying. The distance between them
was too great. She was a banished soul—beholding a possible life which
